reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the CNS
clinicalPearls: A benign glioneuronal tumour (CNS WHO grade 1) that is a classic cause of drug-resistant focal epilepsy in children and young adults
Typically cortical and supratentorial, with a predilection for the temporal lobe
Seizures usually begin before adulthood and are often refractory to medication, prompting epilepsy surgery evaluation
MRI characteristically shows a well-defined, multinodular, cortically based lesion with a 'bubbly' appearance and little or no enhancement or oedema
The histological hallmark is the specific glioneuronal element, with axon bundles lined by oligodendrocyte-like cells and floating neurons in a mucoid matrix
FGFR1 alterations are frequently found and support the diagnosis in difficult cases
Frequently associated with adjacent focal cortical dysplasia, which should be resected to optimise seizure control
reference.pathophysiology: Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumour is a benign, developmental glioneuronal tumour arising in the cerebral cortex, thought to originate from progenitor cells during cortical development, in keeping with its frequent association with focal cortical dysplasia. Its defining feature is the specific glioneuronal element: columns of axons oriented perpendicular to the cortical surface, lined by small oligodendrocyte-like cells, with neurons appearing to float within pools of pale mucoid matrix. Proliferative activity is minimal and the lesion is essentially non-progressive. Molecular studies commonly identify alterations of the FGFR1 gene. Its intracortical location and disruption of local circuitry underlie the epileptogenic behaviour that dominates the clinical picture.
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution brain MRI with epilepsy protocol to characterise the cortical lesion
Video-EEG to localise the seizure focus
Neuropsychological assessment as part of epilepsy surgery workup
Histopathology demonstrating the specific glioneuronal element
FGFR1 and BRAF molecular testing to refine the diagnosis
Careful evaluation for associated focal cortical dysplasia
redFlags: Drug-resistant seizures impairing development, safety or quality of life
Atypical enlargement, enhancement or oedema suggesting an alternative or higher-grade diagnosis
Rapid clinical change inconsistent with an indolent lesion
Features suggesting diffuse glioma rather than a circumscribed glioneuronal tumour
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent, as the tumour is benign and non-progressive; complete surgical resection commonly achieves long-term seizure freedom, particularly when associated cortical dysplasia is also removed. Malignant transformation is very rare, and incidental or well-controlled lesions may be monitored.
pitfalls: Mistaking a DNET for a diffuse low-grade glioma and pursuing unnecessary aggressive treatment
Incomplete resection leaving adjacent cortical dysplasia and resulting in persistent seizures
Overlooking the diagnosis in young patients with long-standing drug-resistant focal epilepsy
Attributing benign imaging change to progression and over-investigating
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
management: Offer surgical resection as the definitive treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy, aiming for complete removal of the cortically based lesion and any associated focal cortical dysplasia to maximise seizure freedom
Control focal seizures with antiseizure medication while awaiting surgery and during postoperative follow-up
Evaluate candidacy for epilepsy surgery with video-EEG, high-resolution MRI, neuropsychological assessment and functional MRI where eloquent cortex is involved
Observe incidental or well-controlled lesions with serial MRI, given the benign, non-progressive nature of this WHO grade 1 tumour
Avoid chemotherapy and radiotherapy, which are not indicated for this benign glioneuronal tumour
Manage within a multidisciplinary neuro-oncology and epilepsy surgery team with long-term seizure and imaging surveillance for the rare recurrence
